title: Data Storytelling and Advanced Visualization
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Data Storytelling and Advanced Visualization ##### The 47-slide deck that changed nothing An analyst at a consumer lending startup in Bengaluru spent three weeks on the best analysis of her career. She had found that borrowers who completed the in-app financial literacy module defaulted at 4.1% versus 7.8% for those who skipped it — and after matching on credit score, income band, and loan size, a 2.3 percentage point gap survived. On a ₹900 crore book, that was roughly ₹20 crore in avoided losses. She presented 47 slides. Slide 1 was a table of data sources. Slides 2 through 19 were her cleaning methodology. Slide 31 had the finding, rendered as a grouped bar chart with eleven categories, a legend on the right in 8pt font, and a y-axis running from 3.9% to 8.0%. Slide 40 was the propensity-score matching diagnostics. The Chief Risk Officer asked one question at slide 12 — "how many customers is this?" — and then checked his phone for the remaining twenty minutes. No decision was made. The module stayed optional. Six months later a different team ran the same analysis and got it shipped with one slide. Her analysis was correct. Her communication failed. And in a data science career, an analysis nobody acts on is indistinguishable from an analysis nobody did. Today is about closing that gap. Not "make prettier charts" — about the discipline of turning a finding into a decision. ##### Why the default output of analysis is unusable Here is the asymmetry nobody warns you about. You spent three weeks in the data. Your audience gets ninety seconds. You know what every column means, why row 40,112 was dropped, and which confounder you worried about at 2am. They know none of it, and — this is the important part — **they do not need to**. The analyst's instinct is to show the journey, because the journey is what was hard. The stakeholder needs the destination, because the destination is what they can act on. Every good data story inverts the working order: ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph WORK["How you did the work"] A1["Data sources"] --> A2["Cleaning"] --> A3["Exploration"] --> A4["Modelling"] --> A5["Finding"] --> A6["Recommendation"] end subgraph TELL["How you tell it"] B1["Recommendation"] --> B2["Finding"] --> B3["Supporting evidence"] --> B4["Method"] --> B5["Caveats"] end WORK -.invert.-> TELL ``` This is sometimes called BLUF — bottom line up front. The Bengaluru analysis, told correctly, starts: *"Making the literacy module mandatory would cut defaults by an estimated 2.3 points, worth about ₹20 crore a year. Here's the evidence."* Everything else is support for a claim already made. ##### The four questions before you draw anything Before choosing a chart type, answer these: 1. **Who is the audience?** A CRO wants money and risk. A product manager wants user behaviour and roadmap implications. A fellow data scientist wants your identification strategy. Same finding, three different documents. 2. **What is the one thing?** If they remember one sentence, what is it? If you cannot write it in fifteen words, you do not yet know what you found. 3. **What decision follows?** "Interesting" is not a decision. "Make the module mandatory for loans above ₹2 lakh" is. 4. **What would make them wrong to act?** Your caveats belong in the story, not hidden in an appendix — but they belong *after* the finding, sized proportionally to their actual importance. ##### Choosing the right chart Chart choice is not aesthetics. It is a claim about what kind of comparison matters. Match the encoding to the question: | Question you're answering | Use | Avoid | |---|---|---| | How do categories compare in magnitude? | Horizontal bar, sorted by value | Pie chart, 3D anything | | How has one thing changed over time? | Line chart | Bar chart per time point | | How is a single variable distributed? | Histogram, or box/violin for groups | Bar of the mean alone | | How do two continuous variables relate? | Scatter, with a fitted line | Dual-axis line chart | | How does a total break into parts over time? | Stacked area (few series) or small multiples | Stacked bar with 12 segments | | How do many groups compare on many metrics? | Small multiples / faceted grid | One chart with 14 lines | | Where does a funnel leak? | Ordered bar with step labels | Pie of final states | Three rules that eliminate most bad charts: - **Sort bars by value, not alphabetically.** Alphabetical order encodes nothing. Sorted order makes the ranking readable in one glance. - **Bar charts must start at zero.** The bar's *length* is the encoding; truncating the axis makes a 3% difference look like a 300% one. Line charts may be truncated, because the encoding is the *slope*, not the distance from the axis — but say so. - **Fewer than seven categories, or aggregate the tail into "Other."** The eleven-category grouped bar on slide 31 was unreadable, and it was unreadable because it tried to answer four questions at once. ##### The redesign, concretely Take the Bengaluru chart. Eleven loan-purpose categories × 2 module states = 22 bars, truncated y-axis, legend on the right. Here is the honest version, built in Plotly: ```python import pandas as pd import plotly.graph_objects as go df = pd.DataFrame({ "segment": ["₹0–1L", "₹1–2L", "₹2–5L", "₹5–10L", "₹10L+"], "completed": [3.6, 3.9, 4.2, 4.4, 4.8], "skipped": [6.1, 6.9, 7.9, 8.6, 9.4], "borrowers": [41200, 33800, 28900, 14100, 6300], }) df["gap"] = df["skipped"] - df["completed"] fig = go.Figure() fig.add_trace(go.Bar( y=df["segment"], x=df["skipped"], orientation="h", name="Skipped module", marker_color="#C0392B", text=[f"{v:.1f}%" for v in df["skipped"]], textposition="outside", hovertemplate="%{y}
Skipped: %{x:.1f}%", )) fig.add_trace(go.Bar( y=df["segment"], x=df["completed"], orientation="h", name="Completed module", marker_color="#1F77B4", text=[f"{v:.1f}%" for v in df["completed"]], textposition="outside", hovertemplate="%{y}
Completed: %{x:.1f}%", )) fig.update_layout( title=dict( text="Borrowers who finish the literacy module default ~half as often" "
90-day default rate by loan size, matched on credit score " "and income · 124,300 loans · FY25-26", x=0, xanchor="left", ), xaxis=dict(title="90-day default rate (%)", range=[0, 11], ticksuffix="%"), yaxis=dict(title="Loan size", autorange="reversed"), barmode="group", bargap=0.28, legend=dict(orientation="h", y=1.02, x=0, yanchor="bottom"), plot_bgcolor="white", font=dict(family="Inter, sans-serif", size=13), margin=dict(l=90, r=40, t=110, b=60), height=440, ) fig.add_annotation( x=9.4, y="₹10L+", text="Gap widens with loan size →", showarrow=True, arrowhead=2, ax=-70, ay=-40, font=dict(size=12, color="#555"), ) fig.write_html("default_gap.html", include_plotlyjs="cdn") ``` Notice what the code is doing beyond drawing bars. **The title is the finding**, not "Default Rate by Segment." The subtitle carries the sample size, the matching method, and the period — everything a sceptical reader needs to trust it. The axis starts at zero. Values are labelled directly, so the reader never traces back to an axis. The annotation points at the secondary insight instead of leaving the reader to find it. A title that states the conclusion is the single highest-leverage change you can make to any chart you have ever produced. ##### Altair when you want grammar, Plotly when you want interaction Altair implements Wilkinson's grammar of graphics — the same lineage as ggplot2, formalised in Wickham's 2010 *A Layered Grammar of Graphics*. You describe **data → mark → encoding**, and the library composes the rest. It is superb for exploratory work and faceting: ```python import altair as alt long = df.melt( id_vars=["segment", "borrowers"], value_vars=["completed", "skipped"], var_name="module_status", value_name="default_rate", ) chart = ( alt.Chart(long) .mark_circle() .encode( x=alt.X("default_rate:Q", title="90-day default rate (%)", scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0, 11])), y=alt.Y("segment:N", title="Loan size", sort=None), size=alt.Size("borrowers:Q", title="Borrowers", scale=alt.Scale(range=[80, 900])), color=alt.Color("module_status:N", title="Module", scale=alt.Scale(range=["#1F77B4", "#C0392B"])), tooltip=["segment", "module_status", "default_rate", "borrowers"], ) .properties( width=520, height=280, title="Default gap persists across every loan size band", ) ) chart.save("default_gap_altair.html") ``` Rough guidance: **Altair** for fast, correct, faceted exploration and for anything going into a Jupyter-based report. **Plotly** for interactive dashboards, executive-facing HTML, and Dash apps. **Matplotlib** when you need pixel control for a paper or a print deck. **seaborn** for statistical exploration at speed. Interactivity is a tool, not a decoration. Add a tooltip when the exact number matters and cluttering the chart would hurt. Add a filter when different stakeholders need different slices. Do **not** add a dropdown because it looks sophisticated — every control is a decision you have offloaded onto your reader, and readers who must configure a chart to see the point usually do not see the point. ##### Structuring the story A stakeholder-ready narrative has five beats, and it fits on one page or three slides: 1. **Situation** — the shared context in one sentence. *"Defaults on the personal loan book have run at 7.1% this year, above our 6% target."* 2. **Complication** — the tension. *"We have tried tightening credit cuts twice; each cut reduced defaults but shrank originations more."* 3. **Finding** — your result, quantified, with the chart. *"Completion of the literacy module is associated with a 2.3-point lower default rate after matching."* 4. **Recommendation** — the specific action, with its expected value. *"Make the module mandatory for loans above ₹2 lakh. Estimated ₹20 crore annual loss avoidance; ~4% of applicants may drop off at onboarding."* 5. **Caveats and next step** — honest limits and how to resolve them. *"This is observational; motivated borrowers self-select into the module. A two-week randomised rollout in three states would settle it."* The **executive summary** is that structure compressed into one paragraph. It should be readable standing up, contain at least one number that maps to money or users, and name the decision being requested. Write it last, after you know your conclusion — and then put it first. ##### How charts mislead Your assignment is to find and fix a misleading chart, so know the catalogue: - **Truncated bar axis** — a y-axis starting at 3.9% turning a 2-point gap into a visual chasm. - **Dual y-axes** — two arbitrary scales that can manufacture or hide correlation depending on where you set them. Use indexed lines or small multiples instead. - **Cherry-picked date range** — a decline that only exists if you start the series at the historical peak. - **Pie charts with more than five slices**, or worse, exploded 3D pies where perspective distorts area. - **Aggregation hiding Simpson's paradox** — the overall trend reversing within every subgroup. - **Unequal bin widths** in a histogram, making one region look denser than it is. - **Missing denominators** — "Maharashtra has the most defaults" is meaningless without "per 1,000 loans." - **Rainbow colour scales** for ordered data, which create false boundaries where the hue changes fastest. - **Area encoding a linear quantity** — doubling both width and height of a pictogram quadruples the perceived value. ##### Common mistakes - Titling charts with the variables (`"Revenue by Month"`) instead of the finding (`"Revenue fell 12% after the March pricing change"`). - Leading with methodology because it was the hard part. - Presenting five findings instead of one; the audience remembers zero. - Not stating the sample size or the time period on the chart itself. - Default colour palettes that are not colourblind-safe — about 1 in 12 men has a red/green deficiency. - Building a dashboard when the answer is a single number in an email. - Using red and green as the only encoding for good and bad. - Rendering ₹ figures without units, so ₹20,00,00,000 has to be counted digit by digit instead of written as ₹20 crore. - Burying caveats in an appendix, which reads as concealment when someone finds them later. - Never asking a colleague to read the chart cold. Thirty seconds of "what do you think this says?" catches most failures. ##### Hands-on: rewrite something you already did The practical task is a good one precisely because it uses old work. Take a past analysis and produce exactly two things: a one-paragraph executive summary that quantifies business impact, and one polished chart supporting the main conclusion. The constraint of *one* chart forces the hardest decision — what is the single thing? The mini project builds the full stakeholder report or interactive dashboard: problem, findings, recommendation, with every visualization deliberately chosen and annotated. Write one sentence per chart justifying its type — "horizontal bar because I am comparing eleven named categories and the labels are long." If you cannot write that sentence, you picked the chart by habit. The assignment — find a misleading chart, explain the mechanism, redesign it honestly — is the one that sharpens your eye permanently. Indian news graphics during election season and quarterly earnings decks are a rich hunting ground. Rebuild it with Plotly or Altair, put the two versions side by side, and write the diagnosis in two sentences. ##### Key takeaways - **An analysis that does not change a decision has no value**, however rigorous it is; communication is part of the job, not a soft add-on. - **Invert your working order when you tell it**: recommendation first, then finding, then evidence, then method, then caveats. - **Chart type is a claim about which comparison matters** — sort bars, start bar axes at zero, cap categories at about seven, and use small multiples instead of spaghetti. - **Make the title the finding.** It is the cheapest, highest-impact edit available to any chart you will ever make. - **Every chart carries its own provenance**: sample size, time period, and method in the subtitle, so a sceptical reader can trust it without asking you.
